drills.q: Explain why BigQuery's scan-based billing fundamentally changes query-optimization thinking compared to Redshift's cluster-based model.
drills.a: Redshift bills cluster size x uptime, roughly independent of any individual query's efficiency -- optimization means right-sizing the cluster and managing concurrency. BigQuery on-demand bills per query for bytes scanned ($6.25/TiB), independent of cluster size since there is no cluster -- optimization means shrinking bytes scanned via partitioning, clustering, and column selection. A SELECT * that costs nothing extra on an already-provisioned idle Redshift cluster directly costs money every single run on BigQuery, because columnar billing has no buffer-cache fallback that makes repeated queries free.

drills.q: Design the partitioning and clustering strategy for a 5-year, 50-column event table queried mostly by date range and user_id, and explain your reasoning.
drills.a: Partition by DATE(event_timestamp) -- daily partitioning covers 5 years well within the 4,000-partition cap (~11yr runway) and matches the dominant date-range filter. Cluster by user_id (and optionally event_type) so within any day's partition BigQuery block-prunes to just that user's rows instead of scanning the whole day. Order clustering columns by filter frequency/selectivity, most-filtered first, since BigQuery sorts by column1 then column2 within that.

drills.q: A team hits query queuing during a product launch, all queries on the on-demand shared slot pool. Diagnose and give the fix options.
drills.a: On-demand queries share roughly 2,000 concurrent slots per project -- a spike in simultaneous queries causes queuing/slowdown from slot contention, not per-query cost increase. Options: buy Editions capacity for dedicated (non-shared) slots, spread load across multiple projects, or reduce per-query cost via partitioning/clustering/materialized views so more queries fit in the same slot-time. Diagnostic order matters: check for unnecessarily expensive unpruned scans before concluding more capacity is the fix -- buying slots to paper over an unpartitioned table is a real anti-pattern.

drills.q: Explain why a materialized view built on a two-table JOIN might silently stop refreshing incrementally, and how you'd notice in production.
drills.a: Incremental refresh for JOIN-based materialized views only supports appended data on the LEFT-side table. Any change (append/update/delete) to the right-side table forces a full non-incremental rebuild -- slower and potentially expensive on large base tables, with no explicit error thrown. You'd notice via refresh job cost/duration creeping up over time as the right-side table churns more. Fix: put the more frequently-changing table on the left, or split into separate materialized views if that's not achievable.

drills.q: Contrast Pub/Sub's default delivery guarantee with Kinesis's, and explain the implication for a payment-processing pipeline needing strict per-account ordering.
drills.a: Pub/Sub defaults to at-least-once with no ordering guarantee unless ordering keys are explicitly enabled (opt-in, same-region-per-key publish constraint); GA exactly-once mode exists as an opt-in, latency-costing feature. Kinesis gives per-shard ordering for free by construction but has no managed exactly-once mode ever -- dedup is always the consumer's job via idempotency keys and KCL checkpointing. For per-account ordering: Pub/Sub needs ordering keys keyed by account ID explicitly enabled; Kinesis needs account ID as the partition key so ordering falls out naturally -- either way, idempotent processing is still required since neither guarantees end-to-end exactly-once for free.

drills.q: A Pub/Sub subscriber with ordering enabled stops processing new messages for one specific customer while all others flow normally. Diagnose and give the mitigation.
drills.a: Because delivery is still at-least-once underneath ordering keys, one message for that customer's key likely failed to ack (transient error, bad payload) and is stuck in redelivery. Ordering guarantees mean every subsequent message for that same key is held back until the stuck message acks -- designed behavior, not a bug, but means one bad message blocks that entity's entire stream. Mitigation: configure a dead-letter topic with a max-delivery-attempts threshold so a repeatedly-failing message gets diverted out of the ordered stream after N attempts, unblocking later messages -- this necessarily breaks strict ordering for that one message but prevents indefinite stalls.

drills.q: Explain why partitioning a high-ingest-volume table by hour instead of by day is often the wrong default, even though it seems to match the ingest pattern.
drills.a: BigQuery caps a table at 4,000 partitions total. Daily partitioning gives ~11 years of runway before hitting that cap; hourly partitioning burns through it in ~5 months. High intra-day ingest volume is what clustering (not finer partitioning) is meant to absorb -- clustering has no partition-count ceiling and subdivides more granularly within a daily partition than hourly partitioning would, without the hard-limit risk that forces an emergency re-partitioning migration mid-retention-period.

drills.q: Explain Dataflow's Streaming Engine and why it specifically enables faster autoscaling, without changing pipeline correctness.
drills.a: Without Streaming Engine, each worker VM holds its own windowing state, timers, and persistent state locally -- scaling the fleet means migrating that state, which is slow and limits autoscaling aggressiveness. Streaming Engine offloads windowing/state/timer management to a separate managed backend, making workers near-stateless so they can be added/removed quickly (1 to 1000+ workers) without state-migration overhead. This is purely an infrastructure/execution optimization -- the same Beam windowing and watermark semantics apply whether or not it's enabled; it doesn't change correctness guarantees like exactly-once processing within Beam.

drills.q: A candidate claims BigQuery must be slow for point lookups because it has no indexes. Evaluate and correct this claim precisely.
drills.a: Correct that BigQuery has no B-tree indexes and is genuinely the wrong tool for single-row point lookups needing single-digit-ms latency (Bigtable, Cloud SQL, or Firestore fit that instead). But for analytical range/filter queries, partitioning (coarse date/int-range pruning) and clustering (fine-grained block pruning within a partition) serve the same cost/scan-reduction purpose an index would, via block-metadata pruning rather than row-level index seeks -- suited to bulk analytical scans, not single-row fetches. Over-tuning clustering to fake index-like point-lookup performance still executes as a block scan, not a true seek, and remains meaningfully slower than an indexed OLTP system.

drills.q: Justify choosing Looker over Looker Studio for a finance team needing consistent metric definitions across 40 dashboards built by different teams, despite the six-figure cost gap.
drills.a: The core problem -- 40 independently-built dashboards risking divergent metric definitions (two teams' 'revenue' disagreeing) -- is exactly what LookML's centralized semantic layer solves: define the metric once, compile to governed SQL, every dashboard/embed inherits it. Looker Studio has no modeling layer; consistency would depend entirely on manual discipline across 40 teams, which doesn't scale. The six-figure cost is justified specifically by the governance requirement and consumer count; for a single team's dashboards that cost would be unjustifiable and Looker Studio would be correct instead. A cheaper partial alternative -- shared BigQuery views -- enforces consistent SQL but lacks LookML's derived-metric modeling and access-controlled self-service layer.

drills.q: Compare Redshift Serverless's billing unit to BigQuery on-demand's, and explain why calling both 'serverless' is misleading in a cost-modeling discussion.
drills.a: Redshift Serverless bills RPU-hours consumed while active ($0.375/RPU-hour, 60-second minimum, 16GB memory per RPU) -- still a capacity-shaped billing unit (capacity x time), conceptually closer to BigQuery Editions than to BigQuery on-demand. BigQuery on-demand bills purely on bytes scanned with zero idle charge and no capacity unit to reason about at all. For extremely spiky, low-volume workloads, BigQuery on-demand's cost curve is flatter and lower since it has no per-active-period minimum the way Redshift Serverless's 60-second floor does -- 'serverless' describes the absence of a cluster to manage in both cases, but the underlying billing mechanics differ meaningfully.

drills.q: Walk through the three layered BigQuery cost controls and explain why none of them alone is sufficient.
drills.a: maximum_bytes_billed is a per-query, pre-execution estimate-based safety net -- catches one runaway query but does nothing against many individually-small queries adding up, and can miss cases where actual execution scans more than the pre-execution estimate predicted. Custom quotas cap total daily bytes scanned at project or user level (200 TiB default since 2025-09-01) -- catches the aggregate-many-small-queries case maximum_bytes_billed misses, but are approximate safeguards, not strict byte-by-byte caps, and reset only at midnight PT. Partitioning/clustering attacks the root cause (bytes scanned per query) rather than capping after the fact -- without it, both other controls just constrain an inherently wasteful baseline. All three stacked is the actual production answer.
